item.title: How Art Can Help Rewrite the Plot
item.description:
Therapy

How Art Can Help Rewrite the Plot

Why the stories that move you belong in therapy.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Bringing the movies, shows, and songs that resonate with you into therapy can open new paths to insight.
  • Art creates a safe distance that allows us to access and name complex feelings we haven't yet put into words.
  • Stories can help us identify rigid, self-limiting beliefs and imagine new possibilities when we feel stuck.
Source: Photo by Matthew Murphy and Evan Zimmerman / Courtesy of Maybe Happy Ending

For 45 minutes, Alice* couldn’t stop talking about robots.

After three months of difficult sessions grieving the end of her relationship and the shock of her partner’s affair, our conversation turned to the analysis of a Broadway musical she had recently seen, Maybe Happy Ending. In the show, which is set in the future, two “Helperbots” (Oliver and Claire) form a bond with each other in a retirement community for discarded technology, as they grapple with the knowledge that they have been replaced by more sophisticated, flashier models. They are essentially living out their final hours in a well-appointed landfill until their batteries run out.

Prior to that session, we had spent a considerable amount of time sifting through a heap of emotions: her fear of dying alone, the dread that she was broken or would never be “good enough” for another partner or desired again, the rage she experienced when she even saw her ex’s name, the shame she carried as she opened up to friends about being newly single, and the pressure she felt to prove to the world that she could make a relationship last.

Alice was looking backward without a happy ending in sight, and she was adamant that a fulfilling romantic future felt as far-fetched as science fiction. She had lost the love of her life. She was no longer desirable. End of story.

“I am that obsolete robot,” Alice told me. “He was my power station. My feelings of accomplishment are context-centric. If I’m plugged into a wall like Oliver, I’m okay.”

Oliver had given her the psychological distance to recognize how much of her self-worth was connected to another person. That session became a key turning point in our work together, one that we would return to many times as Alice began to find strength within herself that didn’t depend on others.

When the Future Starts Feeling Fixed

While the healing benefits of art and the value of assigning films to watch between sessions are well-documented (Niemiec, 2020), I’m interested in the inherent value of devoting time to films, shows, and music that clients bring into the room. Some therapists might consider this filler, rushing you past thoughts on a Rosalía song or a scene from Heated Rivalry, but I see these moments as valuable openings.

In his book The Self Delusion, Gregory Berns explains that our sense of self is constantly evolving based on the stories we tell ourselves about our past, present, and future. We crave a structure that offers us continuity so we create causal links between the past and present (“I am this way because X happened…”), and future scenarios can begin to feel predetermined (“So I am forever going to be Y and Z”). This plot offers us order and a semblance of control over unpredictable events, but we can find it incredibly difficult to step outside the confines of that fixed story

The linear chain of Alice’s script moved from a painful past (I lost the love of my life), to a tragic present (Now that it’s over, I am becoming obsolete), to a sealed future (No one will ever choose an obsolete model and I am destined to be alone forever)

Berns suggests that art offers us the opportunity to break free from that hardened plot. Stepping into a character’s arc allows us to interrupt the brain’s automatic predictive thinking and situate ourselves back in the present tense. By considering her past alongside Oliver’s journey, Alice gave herself more space to write a new story; she could reframe a loss and question the inevitability of her own imagined future.

Max, a professional classical musician, arrived at my office during a dark period of his life marked by an overwhelming sense of guilt that coincided with any form of pleasure he tried to experience: sex, a major purchase, a nice bottle of wine, playing video games, and even receiving compliments would inevitably land him in a crippling shame spiral. The worth of his profession, which he viewed as a pure indulgence for the most privileged, further contributed to his shame. Joy was a luxury that he never felt he earned. Max had not done anything wrong to warrant these feelings, but if he let down his guard for even a brief moment of relaxation, he imagined catastrophic consequences.

When I asked Max if he could think of a piece of music that best embodied what he was feeling, he instantly named Richard Strauss’ An Alpine Symphony (Eine Alpensinfonie). “I feel like I’m constantly trekking up a mountain and I don’t deserve a break. Any pleasure is an unnecessary distraction,” he told me.

Strauss’ score features 22 sections that take the listener on a journey from night to sunrise and night again; he moves us through forests, waterfalls, flowering meadows, glaciers, thick fog, and even a violent thunderstorm as we ascend the summit.

As Max explained the structure of the piece, he initially heard his own struggle in Strauss’ composition. But the more he spoke, the more he recognized that he was missing so much of the layered depth and meaning of the piece. “Strauss gives equal weight to both the light distractions and the difficult moments in the score,” he realized. “I’m depriving myself of the sunset and scenery every day.” He was robbing himself of the rich variations that drew him to Strauss’ piece in the first place.

These metaphors stay with us long after the session in which they were introduced, and they offer us a shared vocabulary we can return to when the same patterns resurface. Alice would talk about feeling “unplugged” or “looking for a wall outlet” as she started dating again, which became a reminder that her previous relationship tendencies were running the show. Max spoke about “waterfalls” and “sunsets” whenever he was able to enjoy the moment without guilt.

Why Fiction Gets There First

Cognitive science helps explain why art can often lead us to insight more effectively than direct questioning. Raymond Mar and Keith Oatley describe fiction as a simulation of social experience in which we can encounter new ways of understanding ourselves. The abstraction and compression of fiction allow us to examine our own beliefs and feelings at a safe distance without the risk of real-life consequences. By attending to someone else’s narrative, we feel freer to process difficult feelings before we claim them as our own.

Recently, a young man spoke about feelings of abandonment in the movie Aftersun before realizing that he too felt estranged and at times neglected by his own father following his parents’ bitter divorce. The film A Star is Born helped a woman living with a partner suffering from addiction understand that she did not need to wait for a dramatic or public rock-bottom moment to set a firm boundary to protect herself. Carly Rae Jepsen’s song "The Loneliest Time" gave voice to the despair of a man who felt trapped in what seemed like a permanent state of grief after a divorce. A year later, the companion album The Loveliest Time arrived, serving as the perfect soundtrack to his foray back into dating.

Any piece of culture can lead to insight if it lets you connect to a familiar feeling. Notice what pulls you in: What moment was so recognizable you held your breath? What character could you not stop thinking about? What song hit so hard you couldn’t stop playing it on loop? What feels like it was written about your most guarded secrets?

Then consider bringing that work into the room with your therapist. Even if you don’t fully understand why it resonates, bring it anyway. As you discuss it together, you may find a new way to say what you have been holding all along.

* Client names and identifying details have been changed to protect confidentiality.

item.title: Why Your Life Matters… More Than You’ll Ever Know
item.description:
Self-Esteem

Why Your Life Matters… More Than You’ll Ever Know

Nearly all of us undervalue the difference we make. It’s time we finally see it.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • My mother spent her last months doubting whether her life had mattered, believing it had been small.
  • Research shows that nearly all of us underestimate our worth, understating how much we matter in this world.
  • We lost our ancestral villages, “social mirrors” that once reflected our worth back to us every day.
  • Without social mirrors, we measure our worth through achievement, and decide we fell short. But we haven’t.
Source: imagedepotpro / iStockphoto/

Mona arrived in this world on December 16, 1940, an early Christmas gift to an adoring family. After 85 remarkable years, on the morning of August 4, 2026, she said one final goodbye, left her body, and returned home.

In the months before, when it became evident her life was ending, Mona and I talked many times about the life she’d lived, and one question troubled her most: Did it really matter? I’ve known Mona for 58 years, so I assured her that of course it did; it was a big life. She’d reply with, I think it’s been small. I haven’t really accomplished much.

I asked her, When your spirit soars and your body turns to ash, what would you like us to do with the ashes? And she would say, Oh, I haven’t really traveled much in these past 60 years; I’ve spent most of them right here, in this house, so just scatter them in the backyard.

I asked, What about a memorial to honor the life you’ve lived?, and she’d insist, Oh no, I don’t want a memorial. She was scared no one would come. (She gave us permission later, and wait till you read what happened.)

Mona’s assessment of her life was completely misguided… and that’s completely understandable. Our consumer culture measures worth through achievement, so when Mona’s accomplishing slowed with age, she felt her self-worth slipping away. But, in reality, it hadn’t diminished at all. As researchers Scarpa et al. (2022) documented in their study of older adults, while Mona’s “occupational mattering” declined after 65, her “interpersonal mattering” grew. Simply put, Mona did less but spent more time with the people who mattered most.

It’s All of Us

This wasn’t just Mona. Looking at the research, we see the same thing at every age: We underestimate how much we matter.

Kumar and Epley (2023) had people perform small acts of kindness, handing strangers cups of hot chocolate, then asked these givers how much they thought the gesture mattered. Every time, givers undervalued their impact, focusing on the act itself (Was it big enough, impressive enough?) while recipients were moved by the warmth and generosity it conveyed.

Boothby et al. (2018) documented the “liking gap”: After everyday conversations, people consistently underestimated how much their partners liked their company. And Zhao and Epley (2021) found the same pattern with compliments: Again and again, people understated the impact of their generous, supportive words.

Across acts of kindness, conversations, and compliments, we see the same thing—people reaching for consumer culture’s yardstick and asking, Was what I said, what I did, good enough? Big enough? We’re quick to decide we’ve fallen short, missing how much we matter in the lives we touch.

What I Discovered in the Days That Followed

In the days that followed Mona’s passing, the truth surfaced.

An in-home nurse, who’d been with us when Mona crossed over, approached me. A native French speaker still struggling with English, she managed a single word, Mama! Yes, I said. Mona was my mother. But the nurse shook her head, as if I’d missed her meaning… because I had. No, she insisted, BIG mama! This nurse had seen what Mona herself struggled to see: She was the beating heart of our family.

A little later, walking down the hill from my mother’s house, I realized I still hadn’t reached one of her younger cousins, Therese. When Therese answered my call, she burst into tears. Oh no! Oh no! she cried, because she knew. Can I tell you something? I assured her she could. I always looked up to your mother. She was my role model. I always wanted to be a Mona!

And that memorial Mom feared no one would come to? Sixty people came, each carrying beautiful stories. By the one measure that actually predicts well-being—sociometric status, meaning the connections we have with family, friends, and neighbors (Anderson et al., 2012)—my mother’s life was enormous.

My Mom simply missed it, because consumer culture never built a vehicle for delivering the message to her.

The Social Mirror

For two million years, things were different: We lived in villages, small bands of 30 to 150, moving each day among the very people whose lives we shaped. The sick mother we carried soup to last night was huddled beside us the next morning, warming her hands at the same fire. The child we steadied through losses early in life was reaching for our hand at the dinner table. Our significance was never something we could forget, because it was reflected back to us daily in the faces (and embraces) of people who were genuinely glad we were here.

But consumer culture leaves all of us without that social mirror. In its place, it hands us a yardstick, a poor substitute, and we measure ourselves with it: How much did I achieve? How far did my name travel? By that measure, we all fall short, because we can never achieve enough to feel valuable… we’re not wired that way.

The simple truth is that most of us live lives that look like Mom’s, contained and local. And yet they are not small, not even close, because to the people we touch, we help hold their world together. We just don’t have people telling us, or telling us often enough, the way a village once did.

Mom tried to fix this, single-handedly. At her memorial, person after person spoke of my mother’s hospitality, and when my turn came to talk, I explained, Mom grew up in a family village, an extended family all under one roof. And what she wanted, more than anything, was to give you that one thing that had always stayed with her: a welcoming so large that you knew you mattered.

On the morning Mom left her body, she told the people gathered around her: When I’m gone, become one family, one village, loving each other deeply, sticking together, and reminding each other, “You matter so much.”

Because each of us does.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy and the Urgent Need for Conversation
item.description:
Psychopharmacology

Lindsay Clancy and the Urgent Need for Conversation

Personal Perspective: The Lindsay Clancy trial highlights the dangers of checklist care.

Posted August 24, 2026

“This is not a public debate about women’s mental health.” So said the prosecutor at the trial of Massachusetts mother and nurse Lindsay Clancy.

Clancy, who admits to killing her three young children in January 2023 before attempting suicide, had been seen by at least six clinicians and treated with 13 medications in four months. She sought help at clinics, ERs, and psychiatric hospitals, even as the medication seemed to make her worse.

So of course, we’re very much having that mental health debate. How could we not be?

Clancy’s defense is that she suffered postpartum psychosis, a condition her defense claims was greatly worsened by inept and excessive medication. By the time Clancy assaulted her children, she’d reported “horrible” intrusive thoughts, emotional numbness, worsening anxiety about her children, and suicidality. And she'd begun hearing voices.

That Clancy was harmed by medication is, I think, a valid argument. Multiple clinicians prescribed at the same time, with little or no coordination; while one diagnosed her with bipolar disorder, another prescribed bipolar-contraindicated antidepressants.

Lindsay Clancy was also, and as tragically, under-spoken-to. The defense attorney seemed surprised by the pages of forms Clancy filled out before seeing her psychiatrist: “Basically they’re all little checks in boxes.” This lawyer, Kevin Reddington, also seemed shocked at the lack of questions from Lindsay’s caregivers, asking clinicians multiple times if it was normal to wait for patients to “just volunteer” information.

In other words, Clancy’s conversations largely amounted to more checklists.

Clancy expressed worry about her drinking but was never asked what she drank. She described feeling unmotivated but wasn’t asked about what. No one seems to have pursued very far what her intrusive thoughts were.

Clinicians assumed that as a nurse she understood the medications they prescribed; she didn’t, sometimes doing dozens of Google searches a night. It was quite a list: antipsychotics, antidepressants, tranquilizers, sleep aids—Clancy's medication eventually left her feeling disconnected from her body; the world around her seemed “unreal.”

A hospital Clancy checked into diagnosed her problem as over-medication and misdiagnosis. A staffer reached out to speak to her nurse practitioner about their findings, but the nurse didn’t return the call, claiming she didn't receive it.

And this mother of young children told many doctors, nurses, and social workers that she felt suicidal, but questions about this seem to have stopped at the standard one of whether she “had a plan.” Clancy was apparently never asked what she imagined happening to her children if she died—though fears for children living without them is a common theme with depressed mothers.

Clancy’s primary psychiatrist, Jennifer Tufts, described observing her “psychomotor” activity as a crucial diagnostic tool, yet only saw her via telehealth. Tufts’ first actual look at her patient was in the courtroom.

I wish I could say this was unusual care. This lack of what psychiatric survivor Dorothea Buck called “conversation” is baked into our mind care system, particularly now, when the "biological revolution" of the late twentieth century guides practice. Symptom lists, generally from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, rule diagnosis, and medication rules treatment.

The methodology is much like a doctor pressing your liver to see if it’s tender. There might be, if the doctor’s thorough, a question about what kind of pain it is. Then the exam moves on. The problem is that the mind is far more complicated than a liver. In the drive to make psychiatry more medical, the field lost its regard for mental content. The emphasis on lists and categories, like “suicidal ideation,” has driven actual dialogue mostly out of the room. But we are all wildly different, and to borrow a thought from Tolstoy, no two miseries are alike.

Lindsay Clancy was refused a hospital stay and declined care from crisis hotlines because she “didn’t have a plan” for self-harm. Clancy came to believe people could hear her thoughts, and that those thoughts might get her children removed from her care.

Whatever she was thinking before her act, and how hard that is to understand, Clancy was clearly wrestling with fears that could never fit into yes-or-no questions or items on a checklist.

Yes, psychiatry needs to respect the biological component of mental states. Postpartum emotions are affected by hormone shifts, and the many physical changes that come with giving birth. Clancy’s reaction doesn’t appear to have been entirely physical; she did well for the first months after her third child’s birth. Her mood changed as her husband ended his paternity leave and returned to work. She faced going back to work as well.

For those who think Clancy’s treatment was unusually shoddy, I don’t. It tracks with decades of my own care. I lived in a town on the West Coast for 30 years and had a general practitioner I knew well and a gynecologist who Christmas-caroled at my house.

The doctor who knew the least about me throughout that time was my psychiatrist, although, like Clancy, I’ve been diagnosed bipolar. I have sat through hundreds of hours of checklist conversations, yes-or-no questions where a symptom arises and is put within seconds into a list or a note, whether it involves something as trivial as absent-mindedness or serious as self-harm.

This isn't unusual care; it's typical, although the right answer for someone in emotional distress may not just be finding a medication, and it may not be prescribing medication at all.

A social worker who worked for McLean Hospital, where Clancy stayed for almost five days, made a viral TikTok expressing doubt Clancy had had any meaningful interactions with doctors there. (Clancy's defense called her as a witness, though the judge ultimately didn’t allow it.) McLean is one of our country’s premier psych hospitals.

Dorothea Buck survived the Nazi persecution of psychiatric patients, which killed many and sterilized others, like Buck herself. Throughout her life she said of psychiatric practice, “As long as we talk to each other, we don’t kill each other.” The stakes are still that high.

item.title: What Life Insurance Companies Know About Addiction
item.description:
Addiction

What Life Insurance Companies Know About Addiction

Want to live longer? Start by taking alcohol and other drugs more seriously.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Drug and alcohol impairment, psychiatric symptoms, and medical harm predict a greater risk of early death.
  • Life insurers treat substance use as an important and powerful predictor of illness and premature death.
  • Treatment, recovery, and sustained remission can restore health and add years to life.

We count steps, track sleep, test biomarkers, take supplements, debate peptides, and search for medications that might slow aging. Yet alcohol, tobacco, and other addictive drugs—some of the clearest threats to a long and healthy life—are missing from this conversation.

Life insurance companies do not make that mistake. Their business depends on predicting who is likely to die younger than expected.

They study thousands of lives, insurance claims, medical records, prescriptions, driving histories, and causes of death. Insurers use these sources, depending on the policy and underwriting pathway. They want to know what a person drinks, smokes, swallows, snorts, or injects to determine insurability and estimate longevity.

A banker in recovery once asked me why a life insurer wanted to know about his former cocaine use, drinking, and addiction treatment. My answer was simple: They want that information to decide whether to insure you—and at what price.

Sources of Health Information

Life insurers collect premiums while a person is alive and pay when that person dies. Naturally, they want to know about behaviors associated with dying early. An insurer may review blood or urine test results, prescription histories, medical records, driving records, and previous insurance applications. Each adds another piece to the risk calculation.

But a drug test cannot diagnose addiction, impairment, or future behavior. It establishes exposure—not a substance use disorder (SUD).

For decades, smokers have paid much higher life insurance premiums because their increased mortality risk is indisputable. After the 1964 Surgeon General’s report established the deadly consequences of smoking, life insurers began separating smokers from nonsmokers. They later incorporated urine cotinine testing to identify recent tobacco use. I remember learning about cotinine testing from a colleague who called me irate and wanted to know if the test was reliable and whether a cigar the night before could have been the culprit after he applied for nonsmoker rates and failed.

Prescription records also require interpretation. Buprenorphine or naltrexone may indicate that someone is receiving treatment. An algorithm may confuse treatment with risk. Clinicians should not.

Twenty Years of Life Lost

A landmark systematic review and meta-analysis involving 12 million people across 24 countries and regions showed that patients with SUDs had the shortest estimated life expectancy, 57 years, or an estimated 21 years of potential life lost.

Munich Re, one of the world’s leading reinsurers, found another disturbing pattern when it compared U.S. mortality data from 2021 with data from 2014. Substance use had become the leading cause of death among Americans in their 20s and 30s and the second-leading cause among those in their 40s. By 2023, drug overdoses accounted for approximately 25 to 30 percent of all deaths among Americans ages 25–39.

Among college-educated Americans, substance-related mortality increased by 25 percent and became the leading cause of death among those ages 30–39.

SUDs increase the probability of premature death. They also cause these deaths in the decades when people should be in their prime—building careers, supporting families, and planning for the future.

The Society of Actuaries reported that the average age at death from a drug overdose was only 45—approximately 30 years younger than the average age at death from all causes.

Munich Re’s own life-insurance claims study showed that prudent underwriting reduced drug- and alcohol-related risk but could not eliminate it.

That is one reason the insurance industry’s conclusions are difficult to dismiss. They are not based on emotion or stigma. They are based on their actual experience with drugs and alcohol—who lives, who dies, what causes death, and at what age.

How Much Drug History Matters?

Major insurers often advise against applying when someone with a treatment history has been drinking or using drugs during the previous year. They also advise against submitting a life insurance application if a person received treatment for alcohol use disorder involving detoxification or inpatient care during the previous two years, or applications involving illegal drug use within the previous three years.

Alcoholic hepatitis and recent illegal drug use other than marijuana may also result in a "decline to insure."

Marijuana is evaluated separately from other drug use. Cannabis-related practices vary by insurer, frequency of use, SUDs, indication, prevailing laws, medical use, and other risk factors.

Driving history matters, too. More than one DUI may make an applicant uninsurable for one or two years, depending on age. A single DUI during the previous 12 months—or more than one during the previous five years—usually affects rates and may also result in a decline.

Insurance guidance also contains an important message about treatment and recovery. Preferred insurance rates may become available after more than 10 years of recovery without relapse. Alcohol and drug use, SUDs, and recovery change the insurance calculus.

Overdose Is the Tip of the Iceberg

When the public thinks about the numbers of drug-related deaths, it usually thinks about overdose. Insurers understand the larger picture.

Drugs and alcohol can shorten life even when an overdose never occurs.

In a separate national analysis of fatal injuries, approximately one in five suicide deaths involved either a blood alcohol concentration of 0.10% (0.10 g/dL) or higher or another indication of alcohol intoxication.

Overdose may be the most visible result of SUDs, but it is only one cause of premature death from SUDs, accounting for roughly 20 to 50 percent of total premature mortality and years of life lost.

Years of life lost from substance abuse
Source: Mark Gold, MD, with permission

Risk

Insurers are very good at identifying risks in large populations. They are less capable of describing individual people's lives. A urine result can identify recent use, but it cannot diagnose an SUD. Prescription data may identify addiction treatment but confuse it with risks.

This is where clinicians should outperform algorithms. We assess patterns of use, loss of control, co-occurring psychiatric and medical illness, relapse history, treatment engagement, changes over time, and engagement in aftercare, which can reduce risk and save lives.

Clinicians may believe we can identify who will succeed in recovery—and would hesitate to deny them life insurance. I have seen many patients in sustained recovery become healthier and more committed to healthy living than ever before. But I have also been overly optimistic. Insurance data confirm that SUDs are often chronic, relapsing, and life-shortening, although some people achieve stable, lasting remission.

Longevity Conundrum

Americans are increasingly willing to spend thousands of dollars on biological-age testing, supplements, peptides, imaging, and other interventions marketed to help them live longer. Eric Topol, MD, one of the leading physician-scientists studying healthy aging, has noted that much of the commercial longevity industry lacks evidence of efficacy. A more important focus is preventing diseases that shorten healthy life expectancy. Substance use is one of those threats.

Conclusion

The life insurance industry's data and experience place drugs and alcohol squarely at the intersection of behavior and longevity. We should listen.

Do an honest self-inventory. Ask not only whether you meet SUD criteria but also whether it’s damaging your sleep, mood, blood pressure, liver, heart, cognition, relationships, or safety.

Addiction can take decades from a life. Treatment and recovery can give many of those years back.
